item.title: Community remembers 17-year-old Lisa, but safety concerns remain
item.description:
Community remembers 17-year-old Lisa, but safety concerns remain

August 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Exactly a year ago, 17-year-old Lisa was stabbed to death while cycling home to Abcoude after a night out in Amsterdam, sending shockwaves through the country and spearheading campaigns to combat violence against women.

Lisa’s body was found beside a cycleway in Duivendrecht, between the city and her home town, where she was pulled from her bike and stabbed to death while she was on the phone to police.

Shortly afterwards, a 22-year-old Nigerian man known as Christ Jude was arrested at a nearby Amsterdam refugee centre. Earlier this year, he confessed to killing Lisa, along with the rape and attempted rape of two other women in Amsterdam.

A memorial organised by a village church and youth centre will take place in Abcoude Thursday, where people can leave notes or light a candle for Lisa.

Family thanks

That community support, said Lisa’s family in a recent letter thanking Abcoude’s residents, has given them the “the security and strength to resume our lives step by step”.

“Not by hiding us, but by continuing with everything that was so dear to Lisa. Let’s laugh, dance, toast and celebrate life as Lisa did—full of dedication, with a generous smile and surrounded by friends,” they said.

Lisa’s murder took place during the Abcoude Festive Week (Feestweek Abcoude), a five-day annual festival that this year will be held from August 25-29. Organisers have consulted with Lisa’s family, and a commemorative event is expected to be included in the programme. The family’s letter thanking fellow villagers will also be distributed in the program’s booklet.

“It is almost unbelievable that it will soon be a year since Lisa passed away. Our world collapsed and the impact on the town was also immense,” reads the letter. “Thanks to all the villagers for the impressive minutes of silence we were able to experience together. Thank you for the hedge of honour you formed during the funeral, we will never forget these moments.”

Moving forward

Since the murder rattled the country and led to national soul-searching on how to protect women from violence, some things have changed.

Municipalities have taken to designing safer public spaces with women in mind, with several adding more lighting and pruning back shrubbery for more visibility.

But for Danique de Jong, it’s not enough. She organized a “We Claim the Night” crowd-funding campaign shortly after the murder that raised more than half a million euro in three days, money that has been spent on policy, education and victim assistance.

“Many of these measures are about reducing the feeling of insecurity: mowing bushes and setting up a lamp. Then we feel safer, but it doesn’t make us safer,” de Jong told RTV Utrecht. “If we only focus on pepper spray, pruning bunches and hanging lighting, nothing will change.”

Mostly at home

While she said she’s hopeful and applauds the changes, she calls for a cultural shift regarding violence against women. “4.5 million girls in the Netherlands had to deal with sexual violence before the age of 18…[with] someone in their environment who does not accept ‘no’”.

That’s because violence against women mostly occurs closer to home. “A girl being murdered by an unknown person or man is very disturbing but doesn’t happen very often,” Roos Koolhof, a healthcare psychologist who works with victims and those at risk of sexual assault for Levvel/Qpido, told Dutch News at the time of Lisa’s murder.

“Mostly assaults happen in a familiar atmosphere—86% of the time—by the neighbour or your stepfather or a boyfriend or a friend or someone they meet on social media.

“What happens more often is a slap on the ass or touching someone somewhere they don’t like,” she says. “And that is what we should talk about so it won’t happen anymore.”

A survey by the youth news program NOS Stories found that many women feel unsafe in certain places and often carry keys to protect themselves against attack.

Christ Jude’s trial is expected to start in Amsterdam in January.

item.title: More permits issued for newbuilds but pipeline is filling up
item.description:
More permits issued for newbuilds but pipeline is filling up

August 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Turnover in the construction trade was up by 5.2% in the second quarter of 2026 while the number of newbuild permits was close to record levels, continuing the strong trend of the last 18 months.

Sales have grown by at least 5% in every three-month period but one since the end of 2024, although the market has cooled off from its peak of more than 7% aa year ago.

Newbuild permits issued in May, the latest month for which figures are available, stood at 10,824 for domestic houses and 2,637 commercial properties. The total figure is the highest since December 2024, when more than 13,600 permits were issued, statistics agency CBS said.

The number of buildings in the pipeline grew to nearly 234,000 houses and 48,000 commercial premises.

Permits are being issued faster than buildings are being completed, which has caused the pipeline figure to grow by around 33% for houses and 25% for business premises in the last two and a half years.

The CBS also recorded a steep growth in costs in the construction sector, with a 97% increase for domestic properties in the last year.

The agency said the spike was partly caused by congestion on the electricity network, which had prompted councils to speed up the planning process for newbuild projects before restrictions on new connections kicked in.

The labour market in the sector remains tight, with 28,600 unfilled vacancies recorded by the CBS. In the second quarter of the year 133 construction companies folded, five more than in the winter months.

item.title: Unemployment climbs to 4% in June, breaking downward trend
item.description:
Unemployment climbs to 4% in June, breaking downward trend

August 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Unemployment rose to 4% in July as the number of people out of work grew by an average of 2,000 a month in the second quarter, according to new CBS figures.

The Dutch government’s statistics agency recorded 404,000 people out of work in July, while the number claiming unemployment benefits increased by 3,000 to 200,000.

A further 3.2 million people between the ages of 15 and 75 – around a quarter of the potential workforce – were unemployed but not looking for work, mainly because they were retired or excluded by illness or disability.

Unemployment grew among men, particularly those under the age of 45, with 4% of men out of work compared to 3.8% in June. For women the proportion fell from 4% to 3.9% during the month.

The biggest increases were in eastern regions such as Twente, the Achterhoek and Gorinchem, while unemployment dropped in eight areas including southern Limburg, Flevoland and Zuid-Holland Centraal.

The total number reached 416,000 in February, its highest level for nearly three years, before dropping in the spring. A year ago 370,000 people were out of work while 164,000 were claiming unemployment benefit.

item.title: NEC hopes hang by a thread after Champions League home defeat
item.description:
NEC hopes hang by a thread after Champions League home defeat

August 20, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

NEC Nijmegen need a miracle to keep their Champions League hopes alive after going down 3-1 in the first leg of their play-off tie at home to Bodø/Glimt.

The Norwegian side showed all their experience as they withstood a second-half barrage by the hosts, while ruthlessly exploiting the handful of chances they created at the other end.

NEC struggled to break down their patient, well-organised opponents, but a late goal by Clement Bischoff gave them a faint hope of overturning the deficit in next week’s second leg in the Arctic Circle.

“They punished our mistakes ruthlessly,” team captain Tjaronn Chery told Ziggo Sport after the match. “It’s going to be a tough away game, but we’ll give it our all.”

NEC survived an early scare when the referee pointed to the penalty spot in the 11th minute after a handball by Bryann Pereira, but the video replay showed that Bodø/Glimt striker Jens Petter Hauge had touched the ball with his hand first.

The visitors went ahead in the 25th minute when Sondre Brunstad Fet finished off a move that began when Noé Lebreton gave the ball away in midfield.

Incisive

NEC pinned back their opponents in their own half while rarely threatening Nikita Haykin’s goal, while Bodø/Glimt looked more incisive on the few occasions when they broke through.

The second goal came from the penalty spot just before half-time after Tobias Stom pulled back Hauge’s shirt as the striker shaped to shoot.

Andreas Helmersen, who had drawn a fine save earlier from Gonzalo Crettaz, gave the goalkeeper no chance with the penalty.

Five minutes before half-time Haitam Aleesami headed in from a corner to leave NEC with a mountain to climb. But the home side refused to give up and got the goal their efforts deserved when Bisschoff touched in a cross by Dusan Tadic with five minutes left.

NEC almost bagged a second when substitute Kevin Kers saw his header come back off the post. But they will now have to succeed where the likes of Manchester City, Atlético Madrid and Inter Milan have failed in recent seasons by breaching the northern Norwegian club’s polar stronghold.

item.title: Online sleuth links Amsterdam’s “Lucky” to Canadian cold case
item.description:
Online sleuth links Amsterdam’s “Lucky” to Canadian cold case

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

An online researcher may have made a breakthrough in the hunt for the identity of “Lucky”, a man who collapsed in Amsterdam three years ago and is unable to communicate. A recent public appeal for information by the police has surfaced a potential match with a missing person in Canada.

An image of “Lucky”, who was also known by the name “Chris the Canadian” to Amsterdam locals, was likened to a file of pictures on the Vancouver Police Department’s cold case unit by someone on Facebook.

John Russell Kennedy, whose missing person’s file photos appear very similar to the one the Dutch police put out, was registered as missing since 1993.

Dutch police said they are considering the tip, according to paper AD, though they also noted that such similarities have been common in prior cases and turned out not to be real matches. “We don’t want to jump to any conclusions at this point, or to give false hope,” a spokesperson said.

Much of what is listed on the Canadian missing person’s case matches descriptions put out by locals who knew the man before his collapse in 2023. He was said to have a North American accent and appeared to have mental health problems.

Vancouver police confirmed they are taking the tip very seriously and said they had made contact with Amsterdam police, according to Anton van Straten, the person who made the connection online and shared it via Facebook.

“Only an official investigation, for example using DNA, can provide certainty about this,” Van Straten wrote in his post. “Now it is up to the professionals to investigate this further. In any case, it didn’t take me three years to find this potential match.”

If “Lucky” is indeed John Russell Kennedy, he would be 67 years old now and missing from his family for almost half his life.

item.title: Number of non-EU dentists in NL doubles in five years
item.description:
Number of non-EU dentists in NL doubles in five years

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The number of dentists trained outside the EU who are moving to the Netherlands to help fill a chronic national shortage has more than doubled in five years, with recent arrivals coming from countries including Syria, South Africa, Turkey, Brazil and Iraq.

One in four dentists now working in the country qualified abroad, according to the dentists’ association KNMT, and in Zeeland more than half were trained overseas.

Figures from the Amsterdam dental school ACTA, which runs the admissions process for applicants from outside the EU, show 120 people are sitting its professional competence test this year, compared with 53 in 2021, the current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported.

In total, 2,287 dentists with a foreign diploma are working in the Netherlands, a number rising by 150 to 200 a year.

Lack of national funding 
The reliance on overseas recruits is partly due to a lack of education funding for Dutch students. Thousands apply but places are very limited. Etienne Verheijck, education director for the ACTA, called that “a policy choice by the education ministry.”

KNMT chair Hans de Vries called it “painful” that motivated young people are rejected by a lottery system, sometimes three times in a row, while the gap is filled from abroad.

The shortage is expected to grow, and the government’s own capacity advisory body has for years urged ministers to open more training places.

Checking your dentist is registered
To work in the Netherlands, dentists with a non-EU diploma must pass a competence test and learn Dutch before they can join the official BIG register of healthcare professionals. Those with an EU diploma need only meet the language requirement.

The healthcare inspectorate IGJ said it regularly receives reports of people performing treatments such as root canals without being registered. De Vries said dentists may work under a registered colleague’s supervision while they qualify, but treating patients unsupervised is improper and potentially unlawful.

Patients can check whether their own dentist appears on the BIG register, which is public and free to search. Dental care in the Netherlands works differently from many other countries, and full practices unable to take on new patients are already a common complaint.

item.title: Dutch boy, 12, seriously injured in fall in Austrian alps
item.description:
Dutch boy, 12, seriously injured in fall in Austrian alps

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

A 12-year-old Dutch boy is being treated in intensive care after falling 30 metres (100ft) while walking in the Austrian alps.

Local media reported that the boy was walking with his father when he slipped and fell while crossing rocky terrain in the Tirol mountain range at 11am on Tuesday.

The pair were descending the Gänsekragen mountain after reaching the 2,914m (9,560ft) summit at 9.30am.

They were walking along a waymarked path towards a mountain hut in Winnebachsee when the accident happened about 500m below the summit as the boy rounded a corner.

The 46-year-old man managed to climb down the hillside to his son, who was lying unconscious, and raise the alarm. An air ambulance transported him to a clinic in Innsbruck, where he is being treated for serious injuries.

Police are investigating how the boy fell.

item.title: Schiphol security staff begin strike action over workload
item.description:
Schiphol security staff begin strike action over workload

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Security staff at Schiphol will begin short work stoppages and deliberately slow-downs in the coming days, after the airport and its three security firms missed a union deadline to ease a workload the unions say has become unmanageable. Travellers could face longer queues as a result.

Unions FNV and CNV announced the action on Wednesday, after an ultimatum to Schiphol and the firms Securitas, I-SEC and Trigion expired at midday. The stoppages will be flagged only a few hours in advance, and the unions have not ruled out longer strikes if nothing changes.

“Nobody wants industrial action at Schiphol,” said CNV negotiator André Quist. “But if employers take no concrete step against the enormous workload even after a crystal-clear ultimatum, they leave our members no choice.”

The dispute dates back to a shake-up in the spring, when Schiphol cut the number of firms running hand-baggage checks from five to three. The switch to new employers affected most of the airport’s roughly 5,000 security guards, whose pay was preserved but whose rosters, shift times, breaks and leave all changed.

Since then, the unions say, workloads have risen and sickness absence has climbed, leaving fewer guards to carry the same load – a downward spiral they warn is getting worse.

In July the unions made eight demands, including longer breaks, two consecutive days off after five worked, a heat protocol for the terminals, and at least two women on every security lane so female passengers can be searched. A lane should close, they say, if only one woman is available.

Schiphol said it regretted the action and took the guards’ concerns seriously, adding that it and the three firms were already working on improvements to five of the eight demands. It said it would do all it could to limit the impact on travellers.

A separate walkout by around 350 cleaners at the airport also happened on Wednesday for two hours around midday in a dispute over reduced sick pay in the national cleaning agreement, which FNV wants Schiphol, as a major client, to help resist.

Ajax fans who want to watch the club’s crucial Conference League play-off match against Swiss club Sion will have to pay €4.99 after the broadcasting rights were acquired by Talpa.

The match, which kicks off at 8.15pm on Thursday, is being shown on Talpa’s pay-per-view channel KIJK, angering many Dutch fans.

The decision also went down badly with Ziggo, Ajax’s main sponsor and one of the Netherlands’ biggest commercial sports broadcasters.

Ziggo has the exclusive rights to show matches in UEFA’s main competitions, but qualifying rounds are not covered by that deal.

The company posted a message on social media site X, formerly Twitter, explaining that Sion as the home club was entitled to sell the broadcasting rights to the highest bidder.

Mededeling voor FC Sion – Ajax#ZiggoSport #Ajax #UECL pic.twitter.com/jQBKOncc3P

— Ziggo Sport Voetbal (@ZS_Voetbal) August 17, 2026

The return leg in Amsterdam next Thursday, August 27, will be screen on Ziggo’s free subscription channel.

On Wednesday, NEC Nijmegen will be hoping to take a step towards the Champions League group stages as they host Norwegian side Bodø/Glimt in the first leg of their play-off tie. The match is being shown on Ziggo Sport, with the return leg in Norway next Tuesday, August 25.

item.title: Criminals cashing in on black market for non-deposit cans
item.description:
Criminals cashing in on black market for non-deposit cans

August 19, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Criminal gangs are earning millions by importing canned drinks to bypass the Dutch deposit return system.

The black market has sprung up since a compulsory 15 cent deposit was imposed on all drinks cans in 2023, as part of the Dutch government’s plans to cut waste.

The environmental standards inspectorate ILT estimates that up to 50 million illegally imported bottles are sold every year, often in restaurants and cafés that buy them from illegal traders.

In an echo of the Netherlands’ cannabis policy, importing canned drinks is outlawed, but buying and selling them after they cross the border is not, making the drinks attractive to outlets that want to avoid the cost and logistical burden of recycling thousands of cans.

Soft drinks are bought from Germany and Denmark, while beer is more commonly imported from Poland, all countries in the border-free Schengen zone.

The result is that the cans end up in landfill or as litter, hampering the government’s efforts to meet its recycling targets.

“It’s an illegal trade,” ILT acting inspector-general Edwin van Houten told EenVandaag. “They come into contact with organised crime because there is a huge amount of money to be earned from avoiding the rules. It runs into the millions of euros.”

Van Houten said the rules were difficult to enforce because only importation is illegal. In the last year 500 inspections were carried out and 90 companies were given warnings, but only five were fined.

“It’s a drop in the ocean and it costs a lot of capacity because we need to do far-reaching, deep investigations,” he said.
